Just now

--

Building a plugin the hard way, one month before Figma made it easy, and what AI is really changing about UX research.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Every UX designer knows this Monday morning.Every UX designer has had this Monday.
You open a research report in one tab, a Figma file in another, and a Google Doc where you’re trying to turn one into the other. It’s 9:30 AM. By lunchtime you have half a persona. By end of day you have a full one that mostly works. You paste it into Figma, style it, and wonder if anyone on the team will actually use it.
I’ve had a lot of these Mondays. A few months ago, I started asking whether we needed to keep having them.
That question turned into a Figma plugin called Smart Persona Generator. It’s free, it’s live, and building it taught me more about AI in UX than any of the AI in UX articles I’d been reading.
Here’s what I learned.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Thirty seconds, one click, one persona card.What I built and why
I built Smart Persona Generator because I couldn’t find a tool that did what I actually needed.
There are AI writing tools that will spit out a persona if you prompt them well. There are template libraries that give you the visual card but leave you to fill in the words. There’s ChatGPT, obviously. But nothing that lived inside my design workflow, on my canvas, using my structure, and producing something I could hand to a stakeholder without ten minutes of cleanup.
So I built three modes into one plugin.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Three ways in. One card out.The first mode is manual. Pick from curated chips for age, occupation, location, behavioural traits, goals, pain points, and motivations. Fine tune each field, or hit “Surprise Me” for a random persona. This is the fallback for when you know your user well but need to get the card built quickly.
The second mode is document upload. Drop in a research PDF or a transcript. The plugin reads it, extracts persona signals using AI, shows you a preview with confidence scores, and pre-fills the form. You review, edit, and generate. This is the mode I use most, because it turns finished research into finished personas in one step.
The third mode is audience brief. Describe your product or user in plain language. Something like “I’m designing a savings app for young professionals in emerging markets who don’t trust banks.” The plugin infers the most likely persona from that, maps it into structured fields, and generates the card. This is for the moments when you don’t have research yet but need to work through possibilities.
Three modes, one plugin, one output. A fully styled persona card on your canvas.
I made the output opinionated on purpose. Illustrated avatar. Representative quote. Behavioural traits. Goals. Pain points. Motivations. Tech profile. Scenario. Persona type labelled clearly as Primary, Secondary, Proto, or Negative. If you’re going to save designers hours, you have to give them a card they’ll actually want to use.

The output. Ready to hand to a stakeholder.The Figma Config 2026 twist
I shipped the first working version in the spring.
A month later, at Figma Config 2026, Figma announced generative plugins. The pitch was simple. Anyone could now build a plugin by prompting the Figma agent. No code required. Just describe what you want and Figma builds it.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Figma’s Config 2026 announcement: prompt to create plugins.I remember watching the announcement and thinking two things at once.
The first was: I could have waited. If I’d known this was coming, I might have built Smart Persona Generator in an afternoon instead of across weekends over two months. Slightly annoying.
The second was: I’m glad I didn’t wait. Because the plugin I built is different from what a prompt-generated plugin would produce. It has opinions. It has structure. It has hours of decisions baked into how the output looks, which fields matter, how the three modes work together. Those decisions came from actually building it, not from prompting for it.
I think this is going to be the thing we all figure out in the next few years. AI generation compresses the making. It doesn’t compress the thinking. A prompt generated plugin will get you to something functional in ten minutes. But the difference between functional and useful still comes from someone spending time on the details.
For UX designers specifically, this matters. Our work has always been about the thinking, not the making. The making just used to be so time consuming that it looked like the job. As AI takes the making down to seconds, what we’re left with is the thinking. Which is what the job actually was all along.
What AI is genuinely good at
Building Smart Persona Generator forced me to be specific about what AI does well in UX research.
It’s brilliant at three things.
First, it’s a fast synthesiser. Give it a research doc and ask what patterns it sees. Ask it to cluster themes. Ask it to draft a persona based on what it read. It’s not always right. But it’s fast, and its wrong answers are still useful starting points.
Second, it’s a good structure generator. If you have unstructured input like a transcript or a brief or a Slack conversation, and you need structured output like a persona card, AI is very good at the translation. Especially when you constrain it, which is what a plugin with fixed fields does.
Third, it’s a decent inferrer. Give it partial information and it can make reasonable guesses at what’s missing. Not always right, but often good enough to critique, which is faster than starting from nothing.
That’s the pattern. AI compresses tasks that would otherwise be slow but not particularly thoughtful. It doesn’t do the thinking. It does the typing.
What AI can’t do (and what UX teams shouldn’t outsource)
Here’s what I learned that made me nervous.
AI is very confident about things it shouldn’t be confident about.
You upload a research doc and it gives you a persona. The persona looks polished. The quote sounds real. The pain points feel plausible. But how do you know any of it is actually in the research? How do you know it didn’t hallucinate a behavioural trait based on statistical likelihood rather than what your users actually said?
That’s why Smart Persona Generator shows you a preview with confidence scores before it generates. You see which signals it extracted and how strongly it thinks they map to the research. You can edit, override, or reject. The AI doesn’t get to decide what your persona is. You do. It just gets you 80 percent of the way there faster.
This distinction matters. There’s a version of AI in UX research that quietly replaces judgement with statistical likelihood. It looks helpful. It saves time. And it slowly erodes the thing that makes UX research valuable in the first place, which is the designer paying attention to what a real user actually said, not what an average user probably feels.
If AI is going to be part of UX research, it needs to be honest about its uncertainty. Confidence scores. Attribution back to source material. Editable outputs. Everything designed to keep the human in the loop, not replace them.
Where this is heading
I think we’re going to see a lot of AI research tools in the next two years. Most of them will oversell what they can do. A few of them will get it right.
The ones that get it right will share a pattern. They’ll compress the boring parts and expand the thinking parts. They’ll show their work. They’ll make it easy for the human to override. They’ll produce artefacts that survive contact with real teams, not just look good in demos.
That’s what I tried to build. Whether I succeeded is up to the people who use it.
Closing
Every UX designer has had that Monday morning.
I don’t think we need to keep having them.
